Here's what your momentum lecture adds:

```
bonsai grow
graph: Energy and momentum
= Momentum
  Momentum is a vector | p = mv points the way the object moves, measured in kg m/s
    > More mass or more speed means more momentum, so it's harder to stop
  Conservation of momentum | Total momentum stays the same when no external force acts
    > Follows from Newton's 3rd law: equal and opposite forces act for the same time
    > Examples: a gun's recoil, ice skaters pushing apart
  = Collisions
    Elastic collision | Kinetic energy is conserved as well as momentum
      > Snooker balls are close to elastic
    Inelastic collision | Some kinetic energy is lost to heat, sound or deformation
      Perfectly inelastic collision | The objects stick together and the most kinetic energy is lost
        > 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest and they stick: v = (2 × 3) / 3 = 2 m/s
graph: Newton's laws
= 2nd law
  Force is rate of change of momentum | F = dp/dt; F = ma is the case where mass stays constant
    > Use dp/dt when mass changes, such as a rocket burning fuel
= Impulse
  Longer impact, smaller force | The same change in momentum spread over more time needs less force
    > Impulse = F × Δt = Δp
    > Crumple zones, airbags, bending your knees when you land
link: Conservation of momentum -> 3rd law | why it holds
link: Impulse -> Momentum | a change in momentum
```
